exam.positive: The defining pattern of primary dysmenorrhoea -- pain outside this window should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis

exam.step: Ask whether the pain has been progressively worsening over months, or is present outside the cyclical window
exam.positive: Either should raise suspicion of a secondary cause (such as endometriosis) rather than primary dysmenorrhoea

exam.step: General abdominal and pelvic examination to exclude tenderness/masses suggesting another cause
exam.positive: Primary dysmenorrhoea should have an otherwise normal examination

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient given the classic cyclical pattern in a young woman with an otherwise normal examination
Reserved for atypical presentations (non-cyclical pain, progressive worsening, treatment-resistant) to exclude a secondary cause

conditions.name: Dysmenorrhoea

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Cramping lower abdominal/pelvic pain tightly tied to the menstrual cycle -- starting just before or with the onset of bleeding and easing over 1-3 days -- without an underlying pelvic disease (primary dysmenorrhoea). Extremely common, especially in the teens and twenties, and often under-discussed. Pain that is NOT confined to this cyclical window, that has been steadily worsening over months, or that is not relieved by usual measures should prompt considering a secondary cause (such as endometriosis) instead of assuming primary dysmenorrhoea.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis based on the cyclical pattern -- no investigation needed for typical primary dysmenorrhoea in a young woman
NSAIDs (e.g. mefenamic acid, ibuprofen), started at or just before the onset of pain -- genuinely effective, not just symptomatic cover
Hormonal contraception if NSAIDs alone are insufficient
Heat applied to the lower abdomen as a supportive measure
Pelvic ultrasound/referral if pain is not confined to the cyclical window, is progressively worsening, or not responding to standard treatment -- to exclude a secondary cause

exam.step: Ask whether pelvic pain is present at times OTHER than around menstruation, not just during it
exam.positive: A genuine distinguishing feature from primary dysmenorrhoea, where pain is confined to the cyclical window

exam.step: Ask how long the pain has been present and whether it has been progressively worsening
exam.positive: Chronic, gradually-established pain over months to years is the classic pattern, distinct from an acute new problem

exam.step: Pelvic examination for tenderness, nodularity, or reduced mobility of pelvic structures
exam.positive: Supportive findings, though a normal examination does not exclude endometriosis

labs.confirms: Can identify endometriomas (ovarian cysts from endometriosis) but a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis
The definitive diagnostic and treatment step, reserved for confirmed/suspected cases needing certainty or surgical management

conditions.name: Endometriosis

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

conditions.summary: Chronic pelvic pain from endometrial-type tissue growing outside the uterus -- classically worse around menstruation but, unlike simple dysmenorrhoea, often present at other times of the cycle too, and progressively established over months to years rather than a new, acute problem. Genuinely under-recognised and under-diagnosed -- diagnostic delay of several years and multiple healthcare visits before a correct diagnosis is well documented, including in India, so pain dismissed as 'just bad periods' deserves a second look if it is severe, chronic, or affecting daily life.
workup: Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal where appropriate) -- can suggest but not definitively rule out endometriosis
Referral to gynaecology for further assessment if pain is severe or affecting daily life -- do not dismiss chronic pelvic pain as 'just periods'
Laparoscopy remains the definitive diagnostic and treatment step for confirmed/suspected cases
NSAIDs and hormonal treatment (combined pill, progestogens) as first-line medical management
Fertility assessment if trying to conceive, since endometriosis can affect fertility

exam.step: Ask about the site (usually one-sided), onset (gradual vs sudden), and any nausea/vomiting
exam.positive: Sudden severe one-sided pain with nausea/vomiting raises concern for ovarian torsion -- a surgical emergency needing urgent assessment, distinct from a simple cyst

exam.step: Ask where the patient is in her menstrual cycle and whether the pain relates to it
exam.positive: Functional cysts relate to normal ovulatory/luteal-phase activity, so timing in the cycle is a useful clue

exam.step: Abdominal and pelvic examination for a palpable mass or focal tenderness
exam.positive: May reveal a mass or tenderness over the affected ovary, though many cysts are not palpable

labs.confirms: The key investigation -- characterises size, structure (simple vs complex) and guides whether expectant management or referral is appropriate
Assesses ovarian blood flow when torsion is suspected -- needed urgently, not routinely

conditions.name: Ovarian cyst

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

conditions.summary: A fluid-filled sac on an ovary, most commonly a benign functional cyst related to the normal menstrual cycle -- often entirely asymptomatic and found incidentally, but can cause one-sided lower abdominal/pelvic pain, either gradually or, if the cyst ruptures or the ovary twists (torsion), suddenly and severely. Most functional cysts resolve on their own within a few menstrual cycles without treatment. Sudden severe one-sided pain, especially with nausea/vomiting, needs urgent assessment to exclude ovarian torsion -- a genuine surgical emergency, distinct from the usual watch-and-wait approach for a simple cyst.
workup: Pelvic ultrasound -- the key investigation, characterises the cyst and guides management
Expectant management (repeat ultrasound in 6-8 weeks) for most simple, asymptomatic functional cysts -- genuinely as effective as active intervention for these
Urgent assessment for sudden severe one-sided pain with nausea/vomiting -- to exclude ovarian torsion, a surgical emergency
Gynaecology referral for cysts that are large, complex-looking on ultrasound, persistent beyond 2-3 cycles, or in a postmenopausal woman (higher malignancy concern at that age)

exam.step: Ask about pelvic pressure/fullness, and whether periods have become heavier or longer
exam.positive: The classic presenting pattern -- pressure symptoms and heavy bleeding, rather than acute pain

exam.step: Abdominal and pelvic examination for a palpable, non-tender pelvic mass or uterine enlargement
exam.positive: Larger fibroids may be palpable as a firm, irregular, non-tender mass

exam.step: Check for pallor and ask about fatigue -- signs of anaemia from associated heavy bleeding
exam.positive: A common, important consequence worth actively checking for, not just the pressure symptoms

labs.confirms: The key investigation -- confirms size, number and location of fibroids
Checks for iron-deficiency anaemia from associated heavy menstrual bleeding

conditions.name: Uterine fibroids

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Benign smooth-muscle growths in the uterine wall -- extremely common (up to 70% of women by age 50), often entirely asymptomatic and found incidentally, but can cause a sensation of pelvic pressure/fullness, heavier or longer periods, and, if large, abdominal swelling. Gradually enlarging over months to years rather than a new acute problem. Iron-deficiency anaemia from associated heavy bleeding is a real, common consequence worth actively checking for, not just the pressure symptoms themselves.
workup: Pelvic ultrasound -- the key investigation, confirms size, number and location
Full blood count/ferritin to check for iron-deficiency anaemia from associated heavy bleeding
Expectant management for small, asymptomatic fibroids
Medical treatment (tranexamic acid, hormonal options) for bleeding symptoms
Gynaecology referral for large, rapidly growing, or significantly symptomatic fibroids -- myomectomy, uterine artery embolisation or hysterectomy are options depending on the individual situation

exam.step: Ask directly about the practical impact -- how often protection needs changing, passing large clots, periods lasting beyond 7 days
exam.positive: No evidence node captures 'heavy bleeding' directly -- this practical framing is how it is actually assessed in the history

exam.step: Check for pallor and ask about fatigue/breathlessness
exam.positive: Signs of the common, important consequence of iron-deficiency anaemia from ongoing heavy blood loss

exam.step: Ask whether the pattern is confined to the days of bleeding and recurs every cycle
exam.positive: Confirms a genuine cyclical menstrual problem rather than irregular/intermenstrual bleeding, which needs different assessment

labs.confirms: The most practically useful test -- confirms and quantifies iron-deficiency anaemia from the bleeding
Looks for a structural cause such as fibroids or polyps

conditions.name: Menorrhagia

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

conditions.summary: Menstrual bleeding that is heavier and/or longer than typical -- soaking through usual protection every hour or two, passing large clots, or periods lasting more than 7 days -- recurring with each cycle. No dedicated evidence node exists anywhere in this checker for 'heavy bleeding' itself (the defining feature), so this is assessed through the downstream consequence of iron-deficiency anaemia (pallor, low ferritin) and the cyclical timing pattern, an honest, disclosed gap. Causes range from fibroids and hormonal imbalance to bleeding disorders -- persistent heavy bleeding deserves proper investigation, not just being told it's 'normal for you'.
workup: Full blood count and ferritin -- checks for the common, important consequence of iron-deficiency anaemia
Pelvic ultrasound to look for a structural cause (fibroids, polyps)
Tranexamic acid during bleeding days -- genuinely reduces blood loss
Hormonal options (combined pill, progestogen-releasing IUS) for ongoing control
Referral if bleeding is very heavy, associated with significant anaemia, or not responding to initial treatment

exam.step: Examine standing up first, then lying down, feeling for a soft, compressible 'bag of worms' swelling above the testis that reduces when lying flat
exam.positive: The genuine hallmark finding -- distinguishes varicocele from a solid testicular mass or a hernia

exam.step: Ask specifically about the onset and severity of any pain, looking for GRADUAL, MILD symptoms rather than sudden or severe ones
exam.positive: Varicocele pain, when present, is characteristically a dull ache or heaviness -- sudden or severe pain should prompt urgent assessment for torsion instead

exam.step: Ask about fever, nausea or vomiting, looking for their ABSENCE
exam.positive: Varicocele is not an infective or inflammatory condition -- their presence points to epididymo-orchitis or another cause instead

labs.confirms: The definitive investigation, confirming and grading the varicocele and excluding other causes
For men with fertility concerns, since varicocele is a genuine, treatable cause of reduced sperm quality in some cases

conditions.name: Varicocele

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Enlarged, dilated veins within the scrotum (a 'bag of worms' feeling), most often on the left side, and often entirely asymptomatic -- when symptomatic, it typically causes only a dull, gradual ache or heaviness that worsens with standing and improves lying down, NOT sudden or severe pain. This gradual, mild pattern is the key distinguishing feature from Testicular Torsion (a genuine emergency) and Epididymo-orchitis sharing this bundle, both of which involve sudden and/or severe, often infective/feverish presentations.
workup: Examine standing up, looking/feeling for a 'bag of worms' texture above the testis that reduces or disappears lying down
Ask specifically about the ABSENCE of sudden onset, severe pain, fever, nausea or vomiting -- their presence should prompt urgent same-day assessment for torsion or epididymo-orchitis instead
Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to confirm and grade the varicocele
Semen analysis if there are fertility concerns -- varicocele is a genuine, treatable cause of reduced fertility in some men
Referral for varicocele repair (surgical or radiological) if causing significant pain, testicular atrophy, or fertility concerns

exam.step: Ask about the ABSENCE of vomiting, fever, or blood in the stool
exam.positive: Colic itself does not cause these -- their presence should prompt urgent assessment for a different, potentially serious cause (pyloric stenosis, intussusception, infection) instead

exam.step: Confirm the infant is feeding and gaining weight normally
exam.positive: A genuinely thriving, otherwise-well infant supports colic; poor growth needs its own separate assessment

exam.step: Ask about the timing pattern -- classically worse in the evenings, occurring in bouts
exam.positive: The genuine, characteristic episodic pattern of colic

labs.test: Growth chart review and clinical examination
labs.confirms: Usually sufficient -- colic is a diagnosis made by excluding other causes in an otherwise well, thriving infant

labs.test: Further investigation only if red flags are present (vomiting, fever, blood in stool, poor growth)
labs.confirms: Reserved for atypical presentations, not needed for typical colic

conditions.name: Infantile colic

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Excessive, inconsolable crying in an otherwise well, thriving infant (classically the 'rule of 3s': crying for more than 3 hours a day, more than 3 days a week, for more than 3 weeks), typically beginning around 2-3 weeks and resolving by 3-4 months of age. DISCLOSED LIMITATION: this checker's age node covers the whole 0-17 range and cannot distinguish a young infant from an older child or teenager, so this doorway is imprecise outside the true infant age range -- always seek in-person assessment for a genuinely unwell-appearing or persistently crying infant rather than relying on this tool. Genuinely should NOT cause vomiting, fever, or blood in the stool -- their presence should prompt urgent assessment for a different, potentially serious cause instead.
workup: Confirm the infant is otherwise well: feeding, growing, and gaining weight normally between episodes
Ask specifically about the ABSENCE of vomiting, fever, blood in the stool, or lethargy -- their presence needs urgent assessment for another cause
Reassurance for parents -- colic is genuinely self-limiting and resolves by 3-4 months in the great majority of infants
Simple comfort measures (holding, gentle motion, white noise); a supervised trial of a probiotic (Lactobacillus reuteri) can be considered per current evidence

exam.step: Confirm the cyclical, premenstrual-only timing -- symptoms present in the 1-2 weeks before a period and resolving with its onset
exam.positive: The genuine diagnostic requirement, though not captured by a dedicated cycle-timing node here

exam.step: Ask specifically about severity and the ABSENCE of severe/acute pain, fever, or pain relieved by defecation
exam.positive: PMS is mild-to-moderate mood/bloating discomfort, not the severe or defecation-related pain of Dysmenorrhoea/IBS sharing this bundle

exam.step: Screen for low mood, irritability and anxiety specifically in the premenstrual window
exam.positive: The genuinely dominant symptom pattern for many women with PMS

labs.test: A symptom diary tracked against the menstrual cycle over 2-3 cycles
labs.confirms: The actual, most reliable basis for diagnosis

labs.test: Thyroid function tests if symptoms don't fit the typical cyclical pattern
labs.confirms: Excludes thyroid dysfunction as a mimicking cause

conditions.name: Premenstrual syndrome

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Cyclical physical and emotional symptoms (bloating, mood changes, irritability, fatigue) occurring in the 1-2 weeks BEFORE menstruation and resolving with its onset -- genuinely very common, affecting most menstruating women to some degree. Distinct from Dysmenorrhoea sharing this bundle: PMS causes milder, mood-predominant discomfort in the days before a period, not the sharp, severe cramping pain occurring DURING one. DISCLOSED PROXY: no dedicated menstrual-cycle-timing node captures the defining premenstrual-only pattern that resolves once bleeding starts.
workup: Ask the patient to track symptoms against her cycle for 2-3 months -- the genuine basis for diagnosis is the cyclical, premenstrual-only pattern
Lifestyle measures (regular exercise, reduced caffeine/alcohol/salt, adequate sleep) as first-line
Calcium and vitamin B6 supplementation have modest evidence of benefit for physical/mood symptoms
For significant mood symptoms not responding to lifestyle measures, an SSRI (often taken only in the luteal phase) or hormonal options can be considered with a doctor

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Rigid, exquisitely tender abdomen
redFlags.message: An abdomen that is hard and too tender to touch or move suggests inflammation spreading across the abdominal lining.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now. Do not eat or drink.

redFlags.label: Possible bowel obstruction
redFlags.message: Vomiting with a swelling abdomen and no wind passing at all suggests the bowel is blocked.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now. Do not eat or drink.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Pain pattern suggesting appendicitis
redFlags.message: Pain settling low on the right, especially if it began near the navel and came with loss of appetite, needs surgical assessment.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day surgical assessment. Do not eat or drink.

redFlags.label: Pelvic pain with a missed period
redFlags.message: One-sided pelvic pain with a late or missed period can mean a pregnancy growing outside the womb, which can bleed suddenly and heavily.
redFlags.action: Take a pregnancy test and go to an emergency department or early pregnancy unit today.

redFlags.label: Sudden severe testicular pain
redFlags.message: A testicle that becomes suddenly and severely painful may have twisted and lost its blood supply. It can only be saved within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now. Do not eat or drink.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Possible diabetic emergency
redFlags.message: Heavy thirst and passing large volumes of urine, with vomiting or deep rapid breathing, can mean the blood has turned acidic.
redFlags.action: Check blood glucose and ketones if you can, and call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Bowel changes needing urgent investigation
redFlags.message: A lasting change in bowel habit with bleeding, weight loss or anaemia needs urgent investigation of the bowel.
redFlags.action: Request an urgent referral and a stool blood test within two weeks.

redFlags.label: Food sticking on swallowing
redFlags.message: Food that sticks going down, especially with weight loss, needs an urgent camera test of the gullet.
redFlags.action: Request an urgent endoscopy referral within two weeks.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
